newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt puts on trial 23 suspected Moslem militants.
newsitem.headline: Egypt puts on trial 23 suspected Moslem militants.

text.p: A Cairo state security court began on Sunday the trial of 23 suspected Moslem militants on charges of plotting to overthrow the government and planning to kill senior officials, police officers and tourists.

Four of the defendants are still at large, including Mustafa Hamza, whom Egypt and Ethiopia say masterminded the failed assassination attempt against Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Addis Ababa in 1995.

The defendants in court pleaded not guilty to the charges, which also include belonging to an illegal group, a reference to the al-Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), and to planning to damage state establishments.
Prosecutors said police seized weapons and money belonging to the group, which they said received military training in Sudan and Afghanistan. It is not clear what sentence the prosecution wants.
"The charges are just the same as in all other trials of that kind," one of the defence lawyers said.
One of the defendants was a juvenile at the time of the alleged crimes, which prosecutors said took place between June 1994 and March 1995.

He is standing trial with the adults despite a new law which says juvenile militants can be tried in special courts with a maximum sentence of life imprisonment with hard labour. The 18-year-old has been in detention for more than two years and his inclusion in the state security trial means he could receive a death sentence.
"As in other cases, defence arguments about trying a juvenile in an adult court were rejected (by the judge)," said Mohamed el-Sawi, a human rights activist.
Two of the prosecution's nine witnesses, all of them state security officers, told the court they did not find anything illegal with two of the defendants they had arrested.
Most of the defendants were arrested in early 1995. The trial adjourned until September 1.
Lawyers complained they had not been allowed to read the case files and had been prevented from talking to their clients.
"We have not read one page in this case and we do not know their conditions because visits are not allowed," said defence lawyer Yehia Ahmed Mutwalli.
"My client has a court ruling allowing him to attend exams at the faculty of medicine, but he was not even allowed to get his books," defence lawyer Mohamed Abdul Qawi said.

One defendant's relative who declined to be named said: "We have not been permitted to visit them (in prison) for over three years." He said there were 10 to 15 defendants in each prison cell and that illnesses such as tuberculosis and skin diseases were widespread.
The defendants looked calm and sat quietly in the court cage, talking in the break with relatives. Some held up copies of the Holy Quran.
The judge, Salah Bodoor, talked to the defendants before the session. One of them told Reuters "Bodoor said, 'You are in fair hands.' But he is well-known for his severe sentences".
The Gama'a has been fighting the government since 1992 to establish a strict Islamic state. More than 1,000 people have been killed in the conflict.
